short: Germany's only tank of the war, of which just twenty were ever completed.
full:
Germany read the Somme as evidence that tanks were a costly novelty, and only ordered a design of its own in late 1916. Joseph Vollmer's A7V — named for the war ministry section that sponsored it — was a 30-ton armoured box on Holt tractor running gear, with two 100 hp Daimler engines, up to 30 mm of frontal plate, a 57 mm gun in the bow, six machine guns and a crew of eighteen. It could barely cross a trench and grounded on rough going. One hundred chassis were ordered but only twenty were completed as tanks; the rest became cargo carriers.

Five went into action on 21 March 1918 near St Quentin on the first day of the spring offensive, and three broke down before reaching the British line. Three fought the first tank-versus-tank engagement at Villers-Bretonneux on 24 April. Germany's armoured strength was in fact largely British: captured Mark IVs, repaired and re-gunned as Beutepanzer, outnumbered the A7V in German service. One vehicle survives, Mephisto, in Brisbane.
